    Summary and Setup

    Working with Ontologies

    A Hands-On Introduction to Creating and Using OWL Ontologies

    Welcome! This practical training introduces researchers to designing, building and publishing ontologies with OWL 2 and linked data. You will apply the concepts as you work through a shared bicycle example, building an ontology and using it to describe and query data.

    Callout

    This training is actively being developed by the TDCC-NES ontology engineers Kathrin Füllenbach and Dani Metilli. If you or your team need ontology training or have feedback on these materials, we’d be happy to hear from you at nes@tdcc.nl.

    Who this is for

    See the learner profile for who this training is for.

    Prerequisite

    Prerequisites

    No prior experience with ontologies, RDF, OWL, the Semantic Web or programming is required. You don’t need a use case of your own to get started: a shared running example is used throughout. All tools used in the training, such as Protégé, are introduced and installed as you go, so no advance setup is needed. See Setup for an overview of the software used in each episode.

    What you’ll learn

    By the end of this training, you will be able to:

    1. Explain what an ontology is, compare it with controlled vocabularies and taxonomies, and assess its value for describing, publishing, finding, integrating and reusing research data.
    2. Explain the relationships and values expressed in a simple RDF example written in Turtle. Describe how Linked Data and OWL 2 can help applications interpret data consistently and support FAIR research data.
    3. Define a research purpose and scope, formulate competency questions (questions the ontology should help answer), and sketch a shared model of relevant concepts and relationships.
    4. Build a small OWL 2 ontology with classes, individuals, properties, domains, ranges, datatypes and logical axioms, using consistent IRIs, labels and definitions.
    5. Check logical consistency with a reasoner, validate RDF data with SHACL, and use representative records to identify and correct modelling problems.
    6. Document and publish an ontology, choose a licence and versioning approach that fits your project, and plan how it will be maintained.
    7. Assess existing ontologies and vocabularies, reuse suitable terms, map your ontology to them, and justify your reuse and mapping choices.
    8. Transform source records into RDF using an ontology, query the data with SPARQL, visualise its relationships and interpret inferred statements.

    How to use this training

    Work through the episodes listed in the schedule below, in order, completing exercises where provided. Each episode builds on the last.

    In this training, we first build a small ontology to understand the modelling choices involved, then explore reuse in depth.

    Episodes marked “Under development” in the schedule are still being written.

    No prior experience with ontologies, RDF, OWL, the Semantic Web or programming is required to take this training. You don’t need a use case of your own to get started: a shared running example (a bicycle inventory) is used throughout. All tools are introduced and installed as you go, in the episode where they are first needed, so no advance setup is required.

    This page summarises the software used across the episodes, so you can install it ahead of time if you prefer, or come back to it if you hit a missing dependency.

    Data Sets

    The Turtle, CSV and XML files used throughout the episodes are provided in episodes/data and linked directly from the relevant episode (for example, the complete bicycle ontology). No separate download is needed: follow the links in each episode as you reach them.

    Software Setup

    Discussion

    Details

    All software below is free to install and works on Windows, macOS and Linux. Each tool is introduced in the episode where it is first used:

    • Build your ontology in OWL introduces Protégé, a desktop ontology editor, with the bundled HermiT reasoner. Follow the Protégé installation instructions.
    • Use and evaluate your ontology introduces RMLMapper (which needs Java 21 or newer) for converting CSV data to RDF, and SHACL Play!, a browser-based SHACL validator that needs no installation.
    • Publish your ontology introduces Python 3.12 or newer with the pyLODE documentation generator, a GitHub account for hosting files on GitHub Pages, and curl for checking published RDF.

    A plain text editor is useful throughout for inspecting Turtle (.ttl) files. You can also use AI assistance to help draft and revise ontologies.

    1. Download Protégé Desktop from the Protégé website.
    2. Follow the installation instructions for your operating system.
    3. The example ontologies in this training were checked with HermiT 1.4.3.456, bundled with Protégé 5.6.7.
    1. Install Java 21 or newer for your operating system.
    2. Confirm the install by opening a terminal (macOS/Linux) or PowerShell (Windows) and running java -version.
    3. Download the standalone RMLMapper JAR (the file ending in -all.jar) from the RMLMapper 8.1.0 release and rename it rmlmapper.jar.
    1. Install Python 3.12 or newer.
    2. Create and activate a virtual environment, then install pyLODE:

    SH 

    python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # On Windows PowerShell: .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install pylode==3.6.1
